title: The breath gets up to leave
hook: in an Upanishad the body's powers argue over who holds it up, until the breath gets up to leave
carry: prana is life, not just air
tomorrow: Why does yoga put the breath fourth?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita ended on one word, kva, where: the self was never bound. And the lineage track closed: karma, bhakti, jnana. Today, a new stretch: practices, deeper.
screen: `THE ASHTAVAKRA GITA, COMPLETE.` · `THE SELF WAS NEVER BOUND.` · `NOW: PRACTICES, DEEPER.`

segments.voice: The powers of the body are having an argument. Speech says it holds the body up. The eye says no, it does. The ear, the mind, the elements themselves all make the same boast. It's a scene from the Prashna Upanishad, told by a teacher named Pippalada to a student who asked which powers keep a living being going. In the middle of the shouting, one power gives a single warning and stops arguing. The breath. Prana. Nobody believes it, so it simply gets up, as if to leave.
screen: `THE BODY'S POWERS ARGUE.` → `EACH ONE BOASTS.` → `THE BREATH GETS UP TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's what happens next, in paraphrase. Prana, the chief power, has warned them: don't be fooled, I'm the one holding this body together. They don't believe it, so prana rises to go. As it rises, every other power is pulled up with it, helpless to stay. When it settles back down, they all settle, like bees that rise when the king bee rises and settle when it settles. Speech, mind, eye and ear turn to prana and praise it. That's one of the Upanishads' big teachings: prana isn't just air. It's the life-power itself, the one the senses and the mind ride on. In Sanskrit the same word means breath and life. That's why pranayama, working with prana by way of the breath, sits inside Hindu prayer and not only in yoga class: the traditional daily sandhya rite, for those who keep it, sets its prayers between rounds of pranayama. If everything rises and settles with the breath, then working with the breath works with the rest too: the restless mind, the racing heart. This week takes the practices in order, gentle ones before stronger ones. Two warnings belong at the start. Breath practice is done gently: nothing forced, nothing held until it hurts. If there's dizziness or strain, stop and breathe normally. And anyone with a heart or lung condition, or who is pregnant, talks to a doctor before trying the stronger practices. Just the king bee, rising and settling, and everything else going with it.
screen: `PRANA RISES; EVERYTHING RISES.` · `LIKE BEES WITH THE KING BEE.` · `PRANA: BREATH, AND LIFE ITSELF.` · `PRANAYAMA SITS INSIDE HINDU PRAYER.` · then, large: `GENTLY. NOTHING FORCED.`

segments.voice: Sit with the spine easy and watch the breath rise and settle without changing it, noticing what goes with it: the belly, the ribs, the shoulders, even the thoughts. After a while, let the out-breath become just a little slower than before, still easy. If you pray, you can let one slow Om ride the last out-breath, the way many Hindus begin their prayers. If anything strains, let it go back to normal.
Pranayama sequences: breath practices set in an order, working with prana, the life the other powers rise and settle with.
Your line: prana is life, not just air. When the breath settles, everything settles with it. Rest well.
